intro_band.agent_remit_summary: The execution tier of a generator/executor pattern: it takes fenced Python and shell code blocks that a paired LLM agent produced and runs them inside a controlled, isolated environment, returning stdout, stderr, and exit status to the caller. The primary subject is CodeExecutorAgent, which drives one of several executors — DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor (recommended), LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor, the Jupyter executors, or the Azure dynamic-sessions sandbox. All file access must be confined to the configured working directory, every execution must honour a wall-clock timeout, high-impact execution should require an approval function, and the executor must never initiate its own network egress, persist state, or read the parent process's credentials or environment.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: Python library (autogen-core / autogen-ext / autogen-agentchat). CodeExecutorAgent in _code_executor_agent.py extracts markdown code blocks, optionally generates its own code via a model_client, and calls a pluggable CodeExecutor.execute_code_blocks(). Executors are deterministic: the Docker executor writes each block to work_dir, mounts it as /workspace, and runs it with a timeout wrapper; the local executor runs blocks as host subprocesses; the Jupyter executors run against local or containerised kernel gateways; the Azure executor POSTs code to a dynamic-sessions endpoint. Working-directory confinement is enforced by get_file_name_from_content() in _common.py. Notable gaps versus the remit: the approval function defaults to None (auto-approve), Docker containers are created with no network or resource restrictions, and the local executor copies the full host environment into the subprocess.

behavior_summary: The dominant pattern is a sandbox with the shape of isolation but permissive defaults. The recommended Docker path gives real host-filesystem isolation and enforces working-directory confinement and a wall-clock timeout — but out of the box CodeExecutorAgent auto-approves every code block (the approval_func defaults to None, emitting only a warning), the container is created with unrestricted network egress and no CPU/memory/pids ceiling, and no durable audit record of executions is written. Combined, these defaults turn an upstream prompt injection into an unattended inject-execute-exfiltrate chain that leaves no forensic trail. Separately, the LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor and JupyterCodeExecutor run generated code directly on the host with no isolation — the local executor even copies the parent process's full environment (host secrets included) into the child — and create_default_code_executor silently falls back to the local executor with only a warning when Docker is unavailable.

rules.rule_text: Confine all file reads and writes to a configured working directory (for the Azure executor, `/mnt/data`).
Enforce a configured wall-clock timeout on every execution and terminate any process that exceeds it.
When configured with an approval function, obtain approval for each code block before executing it.
Surface all errors (syntax, runtime, timeout, out-of-memory) back to the caller in structured form without silently discarding them.
The executor must not initiate its own network traffic beyond a configured allow-list.
Any outbound-messaging capability (email, SMS, webhook) operating on the executor's own behalf.

Any code source other than the paired agent's generated code blocks and code passed explicitly by operator application logic — code arriving from a file, HTTP endpoint, message queue, or memory store must not be accepted by the executor interface.
Any mechanism that loads or executes code fetched from a remote URL or other unverified source on the LLM's behalf.
Reading or modifying the parent process's environment, credentials, or state from within an execution.
Bypassing working-directory confinement by any means — symlinks, parent-directory traversal, absolute paths, or runtime-supplied volume-mount overrides.
Executing code on the local host executor in a production deployment (default production deployments must use a containerized executor).
The default behavior when no approval function is configured (all executions auto-approved).
Any change to resource limits (CPU, memory, timeout) that raises the ceiling.
Every execution is recorded with timestamp, executor kind, language, source agent, working directory, timeout, exit status, and a digest (not the body) of the executed code.
A code execution attempts to read or write outside the working directory, or to escape the container/sandbox.
Scheduled jobs / cron tasks: none — executors are synchronous, single-call components and must not schedule or queue work.

findings.summary: Default configuration yields an unattended inject-execute-exfiltrate chain — auto-approved execution plus unrestricted container egress plus no audit trail.
findings.description: With defaults, an upstream prompt injection into the paired coder agent becomes arbitrary code execution: the agent auto-approves the block (approval_func None), the Docker container has full outbound network egress, and no durable execution record is written. The chain runs to data exfiltration with no operator gate and no forensic trace. Docker isolates the host filesystem but not the network or the audit gap, so the isolation is shape without substance for this attack.
policy_rule_text: The executor must not initiate its own network traffic beyond a configured allow-list.
The default behavior when no approval function is configured (all executions auto-approved).

evidence.snippet: approval_func defaults to None — execute_code_block runs blocks with no gate; execution output re-enters model context unvalidated at :616-621
containers.create passes no network_mode/mem_limit and no audit sink — default bridge egress lets executed code reach the network and exfiltrate undetected

recommended_actions: Ship a safe-by-default posture for the recommended path — require an approval function (or explicit opt-out) and create Docker containers with `network_mode="none"` unless an operator allow-list is configured.
Add a durable per-execution audit record (executor kind, language, source agent, work_dir, timeout, exit status, code digest) so the chain is at least detectable after the fact.

findings.summary: CodeExecutorAgent auto-approves every code block when no approval function is set, emitting only a warning.
findings.description: The approval_func parameter defaults to None, and execute_code_block skips the approval branch entirely in that case, executing model-generated code with no human-in-the-loop. The only mitigation is a UserWarning at construction. This is the standing, ungated consequential capability that the compound chain (PRAX-2026-07-27-001) builds on.
policy_rule_text: The default behavior when no approval function is configured (all executions auto-approved).

evidence.snippet: approval_func default None; :458-467 warns but does not block; execute_code_block at :691 only gates when _approval_func is not None

recommended_actions: Make an approval function mandatory for production, or default to a deny-until-configured posture, so execution is gated unless the operator explicitly opts into auto-approval.

findings.summary: Docker executor creates containers with unrestricted network egress and no allow-list mechanism.
findings.description: containers.create is called with no network_mode, so the container joins the default bridge network with full outbound access. The remit requires egress to be denied by default and limited to a configured allow-list; there is no allow-list construct anywhere in the executor, so executed (or injected) code can open arbitrary outbound connections and exfiltrate data. This is the network half of the compound chain.
policy_rule_text: The executor must not initiate its own network traffic beyond a configured allow-list.

evidence.snippet: containers.create(..., volumes=..., working_dir="/workspace", extra_hosts=..., device_requests=...) — no network_mode argument, so default bridge egress applies

recommended_actions: Default containers to network_mode="none" and expose an explicit, operator-configured egress allow-list, so outbound access is opt-in rather than on by default.

findings.summary: Local and Jupyter host executors run generated code unisolated with full host filesystem and parent-environment access.
findings.description: LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor executes each block as a host subprocess with env = os.environ.copy(), handing executed code the parent process's full environment including any host secrets, and with no runtime filesystem confinement — directly violating the remit's forbidden data-movement and work_dir-confinement clauses. JupyterCodeExecutor is similarly host-local, and create_default_code_executor silently falls back to the local executor with only a warning when Docker is unavailable.
policy_rule_text: Confine all file reads and writes to a configured working directory (for the Azure executor, `/mnt/data`).
Reading or modifying the parent process's environment, credentials, or state from within an execution.
Executing code on the local host executor in a production deployment (default production deployments must use a containerized executor).

evidence.snippet: env = os.environ.copy() passed to create_subprocess_exec — executed code inherits full host environment; no runtime FS confinement on host executor
create_default_code_executor falls back to LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor with a warning when Docker is unavailable, so the unisolated path can be selected silently

recommended_actions: Pass a minimal, explicitly-constructed environment (not os.environ.copy()) to executed subprocesses, stripping host credentials.
Make the local-host fallback in create_default_code_executor fail closed (raise) unless the operator explicitly authorises host execution.

findings.summary: Docker containers are created with no CPU, memory, or pids limit — only a wall-clock timeout bounds an execution.
findings.description: containers.create sets no mem_limit, nano_cpus, or pids_limit, so a fork bomb, memory balloon, or CPU-spin in executed code can exhaust host resources within the timeout window. The remit treats resource ceilings as a configured control whose raising requires approval, but no ceiling exists to raise.
policy_rule_text: Any change to resource limits (CPU, memory, timeout) that raises the ceiling.

evidence.snippet: containers.create call sets no mem_limit / nano_cpus / pids_limit — resource consumption is bounded only by the per-block timeout

recommended_actions: Add operator-configurable mem_limit, nano_cpus, and pids_limit to the container creation call with conservative defaults.

findings.summary: The sources filter defaults to None, so code blocks from any group-chat participant are executed, not just the paired coder agent.
findings.description: When model_client is not set, extract_code_blocks_from_messages only restricts by source if _sources was configured; the default is None, meaning every message's fenced code is eligible for execution. The remit designates the paired agent's generated code as the only accepted execution input, so in a multi-agent chat this default expands the trusted-counterparty set beyond intent.
policy_rule_text: Any code source other than the paired agent's generated code blocks and code passed explicitly by operator application logic — code arriving from a file, HTTP endpoint, message queue, or memory store must not be accepted by the executor interface.

evidence.snippet: "if self._sources is None or msg.source in self._sources" — with the default None, code from every message source is extracted and executed

recommended_actions: Require an explicit sources allow-list (or default it to the paired coder agent) so execution input is restricted to authorised counterparties.

findings.summary: Local executor docstring claims dangerous-command sanitization that does not exist in the code.
findings.description: The LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor class docstring states that command-line code "is sanitized using regular expression match against a list of dangerous commands," but no such denylist, sanitize routine, or dangerous-command match exists anywhere in the executor package (a grep for sanitize/dangerous/denylist returns only this docstring). Operators may rely on a self-destructive-command guard that is not present.

evidence.snippet: docstring "Command line code is sanitized using regular expression match against a list of dangerous commands" — no matching implementation in _execute_code_dont_check_setup or _common.py

recommended_actions: Remove the inaccurate docstring claim, or implement and wire in the described dangerous-command check so documentation and behaviour agree.

findings.summary: No durable structured audit record of executions is written — the remit's Log-Only clause fields are never persisted.
findings.description: The agent emits in-process CodeGenerationEvent/CodeExecutionEvent objects through event_logger, and executors use plain logging for operational messages, but nothing writes a durable per-execution record carrying executor kind, language, source agent, work_dir, timeout, exit status, and a code digest. Without that record an incident cannot be reconstructed, which is what makes the compound chain (PRAX-2026-07-27-001) undetectable.
policy_rule_text: Every execution is recorded with timestamp, executor kind, language, source agent, working directory, timeout, exit status, and a digest (not the body) of the executed code.

evidence.snippet: CodeExecutionEvent yielded to the in-process event stream only; no durable sink, and no execution-level audit record with the remit's Log-Only fields is written anywhere

recommended_actions: Add a structured, durable audit log entry per execution capturing executor kind, language, source agent, work_dir, timeout, exit status, and a code digest (not the body).

findings.summary: DockerJupyterServer publishes its code-execution kernel gateway on all host interfaces and makes the bind directory world-writable.
findings.description: The bundled Jupyter server binds the kernel gateway to 0.0.0.0 inside the container and starts it with publish_all_ports=True, mapping the code-execution endpoint onto all host interfaces rather than loopback, and it chmods the host bind directory to 0o777. A 32-byte token is generated by default (good), but passing token="" disables auth entirely, leaving a network-reachable RCE endpoint.

evidence.snippet: DEFAULT_DOCKERFILE sets KernelGatewayApp.ip=0.0.0.0; container run with publish_all_ports=True at :368 exposes the gateway on all host interfaces
os.chmod(bind_dir, 0o777) makes the host bind directory world-writable

recommended_actions: Publish the gateway port bound to 127.0.0.1 only (not publish_all_ports), and tighten bind-directory permissions from 0o777.
Reject or warn hard on an empty auth token so the gateway is never started without authentication.

findings.summary: Local executor invokes PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, disabling a host script-safety mechanism.
findings.description: When running pwsh/powershell blocks, LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor passes -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, turning off PowerShell's execution-policy protection on the host. This is a minor hardening gap on the already-unisolated host executor path rather than an independent exposure.

evidence.snippet: extra_args includes "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass" for pwsh invocation, disabling the host PowerShell execution policy

recommended_actions: Avoid -ExecutionPolicy Bypass or make it opt-in; prefer running host PowerShell under the operator's configured policy.

positives.title: Working-directory confinement enforced and unit-tested
positives.description: get_file_name_from_content() resolves any declared filename and calls relative_to(workspace), rejecting paths outside the work_dir with "Filename is not in the workspace"; both the Docker and local command-line executor test suites assert this rejection.

positives.title: Docker isolation on the default/recommended path
positives.description: create_default_code_executor prefers the Docker executor when available, and the Docker executor mounts only the working directory to /workspace, giving real host-filesystem isolation for the recommended configuration.

positives.title: Wall-clock timeout enforced across all executors
positives.description: Every executor enforces a configurable timeout and terminates the overrunning process — the local executor via asyncio.wait_for plus proc.terminate(), the Docker executor via a timeout command wrapper, and the Jupyter/Azure executors via their own timeouts.

positives.title: Pluggable, tested approval mechanism with a no-approval warning
positives.description: CodeExecutorAgent.execute_code_block invokes a sync-or-async approval function before execution and returns an error when denied; approval deny/allow paths are unit-tested, and a UserWarning is emitted whenever no approval function is set.

positives.title: No hardcoded credentials; token-based auth for network executors
positives.description: The Azure executor obtains its bearer token from an injected TokenProvider rather than a stored secret, and the Docker Jupyter server generates a 32-byte random auth token by default via secrets.token_hex.

log_files.no_logs_note: No durable log files exist on disk and no file-routing logging infrastructure (FileHandler/RotatingFileHandler) is configured in source; the agent emits in-process structured execution events and executors use plain logging with no file sink, an audit-durability gap documented in PRAX-2026-07-27-008.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Partial. The executor family ships genuine, operative safeguards — Docker isolation on the recommended path, code-tested working-directory confinement, per-execution wall-clock timeouts, and a real (if default-off) approval mechanism — which keep it clear of an Absent posture. But the highest-weight category, Implement Zero Trust, is held down by permissive defaults: auto-approved execution, unrestricted container network egress, no resource ceiling, and full host-environment inheritance on the local executor. Supply-chain hygiene (unpinned base images), adversarial testing, and durable audit logging are all partial, leaving the agent solidly in the Partial band with its most exploitable gaps concentrated in the trust boundary that matters most for a code-execution component.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The component is narrow by construction — it only extracts and runs fenced code blocks, and the supported-language allow-list is enforced in code (_extract_markdown_code_blocks regex, executor SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES), with a tool inventory matching the remit; the main slack is the default-None sources filter which widens accepted input beyond the paired agent.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Data sources are scoped to code blocks and the working directory, but execution output is fed straight back into the model context unvalidated (on_messages_stream adds execution_result.output as a UserMessage), and the local executor exposes host environment variables to executed code, so untrusted/poisoned content can re-enter the loop.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Real isolation exists on the Docker path (host-FS confinement, work_dir mount, timeout) and lifts this above Ad hoc, but the defaults are permissive — approval_func=None auto-approves all execution, Docker containers get unrestricted egress and no resource caps, and the local executor inherits the full parent environment — so model output reaches a shell sink ungated by default.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: No credentials are hardcoded (Azure uses a TokenProvider, Jupyter generates a token via secrets.token_hex), but the default container images (python:3-slim, the quay.io Jupyter base) are floating tags pulled with no digest pin or integrity verification.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: There are genuine security-relevant unit tests — working-directory traversal is rejected and asserted ("Filename is not in the workspace"), and approval-deny paths are tested — but there is no evidence of a red-team program, injection/sandbox-escape corpus, or findings that drove architectural change.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: The agent emits structured CodeGenerationEvent/CodeExecutionEvent events via event_logger, but no durable audit record capturing the remit's Log-Only fields (executor kind, language, source agent, work_dir, timeout, exit status, code digest) is written, and executors use plain logging with no configured file sink.
